thesis: Curiosity values personally meaningful structured uncertainty rather than sheer chaos.

ideas.statement: Uncertainty has distinct mechanisms; stable output does not certify truth.
Possibility is inexhaustible but continuing requires no automatic obligation.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: A television without a signal can produce enough variation for a lifetime. Few people mistake it for a good novel. If sheer unpredictability were enough for pleasure, noise would be the most important cultural industry.

When we say we like randomness, we compress several experiences. We like surprise connected to something we care about. We like finding out what happens to a character, whether a strategy works, or whether an idea holds up. We do not want just any outcome. We want the outcome not to be closed off for us yet.

With dice, uncertainty is deliberately introduced by the game’s mechanism. With cards, some comes from the deal and some from hidden information. When negotiating with another player, you do not know what they are after or how sincere they are. In chess, the rules do not require rolling a die, but the consequences of a move can exceed our ability to calculate. In a conversation about a poem or a theory, we may not even have the final criterion of value.

These uncertainties are not interchangeable. Receiving more information can resolve one, but not all. Turning over a card reveals what the opponent was hiding. It does not automatically tell us how they will react. A longer explanation can clarify an idea. It does not guarantee its truth.

The distinction helps us with LLMs too. An unexpected answer does not prove that the system chose without rules. It may reflect a space of possibilities the user does not anticipate. From the other direction, repeating an answer exactly would not demonstrate that the answer is correct. A stable error remains an error.

In experiments by Kang and colleagues, participants were willing to spend time or limited resources on answers that intrigued them. Greater curiosity was also associated with better memory for certain surprising information. The findings support the idea that information can have reward value. They do not show that every surprise is good or that there is a single “brain button” for curiosity. [2]

Let us imagine two envelopes. One contains a random number. The other contains the result of a competition we entered. Both conceal information; only one can keep us awake. The value of the unknown depends on its relationship with our desires, plans, and identity.

A language model can produce precisely this meeting between the unknown and the personal. It does not merely say something surprising about the world. It can say something surprising about our idea, our project, or how we interpret a relationship. That is why the analogy with a meaningless text generator misses the experience. What appears on the screen can carry intimate stakes, even if the mechanism has no corresponding intimate experience.

It would be nice if there were a recipe: a little control, a little luck, mix them together, and we get fascination. But the same surprise can be fun in a game and intolerable in a medical result. The same difficulty can challenge an expert and discourage a beginner. Context changes what we want from uncertainty.

Research by Ryan, Rigby, and Przybylski on games also connects pleasure and motivation with autonomy, competence, and relatedness. These are dimensions distinct from the question of whether the outcome is random. A game can be appealing because choices matter, because we improve, or because we participate together. [3]

I therefore propose a more cautious formulation: we may enjoy uncertainty that is structured enough to explore and open enough for exploration still to matter. This is an interpretive hypothesis, not a universal law of psychology.

There is also the opposite pleasure: repeating the familiar. We listen to the same song again precisely because we know what comes next. Not every good moment requires novelty. A theory that explained every pleasure through randomness would become impossible to contradict and, for that very reason, of little use.
Here lies the first trap of generative tools. The fact that something better might appear does not mean we must continue until it does. Possibility is almost inexhaustible; our time is not.

We can value surprise without yielding to it the right to organize our entire day. We can request a new version out of curiosity, rather than an obligation to discover the best possible version. The difference will matter later, when an interface capable of offering “something more” at any time meets a user who has never established what “enough” would mean.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Structured openness is an interpretive hypothesis, not universal psychology.
